title: The Dove and the Raven
lead: The two birds Noah sent from the ark (Genesis 8:6–12) became two of the Bible's richest pictures. The dove stands for gentleness, love and the Holy Spirit, who came down on Jesus "like a dove" (Mark 1:10). The raven, an unclean bird and a scavenger of ruins, is still a creature God feeds, and one he used to feed Elijah (1 Kings 17:6; Luke 12:24).

sections.b: Noah first sends out the raven, which goes "going and coming back, until the waters were dried up off the earth" (Genesis 8:7). Then he sends the dove three times: it finds no place to rest and comes back; it returns with "a fresh-torn olive leaf in its mouth" (Genesis 8:11); and the third time it does not come back. Jewish readers asked why the raven failed. In the Talmud, Reish Lakish imagines the raven arguing with Noah that he sent an unclean bird, of which there was only one pair, instead of a clean one (Bavli Sanhedrin 108b). Rashi gives a midrash that the raven was being kept for a later errand, feeding Elijah (Rashi on Genesis 8:7). 1 Peter makes the Flood waters a picture of baptism, through which "a few, eight souls, were carried safe through water" (1 Peter 3:20).

The Hebrew yonah is also the prophet Jonah's name. Doves were the offering of the poor: a mother who could not afford a lamb brought "two turtledoves or two young doves" (Leviticus 12:8), as Mary and Joseph did (Luke 2:24). The dove is the beloved in love poetry: "My dove, in the clefts of the rock" (Song of Songs 2:14). It is a picture of longing to escape (Psalm 55:6), but also of foolishness: "Ephraim has turned into a dove: silly, no mind of its own" (Hosea 7:11). Jesus tells his disciples to be "sharp like snakes and pure like doves" (Matthew 10:16). At his baptism all four Gospels say the Spirit came down "like a dove" (Matthew 3:16; Mark 1:10; John 1:32), and Luke adds "in bodily shape" (Luke 3:22), pointing to something seen. Readers have linked the scene to creation, where "God's Spirit fluttered over the face of the waters" (Genesis 1:2); in the Talmud Ben Zoma says the Spirit hovered there "like a dove hovering over its young" (Bavli Chagigah 15a).

sections.b: The raven is on Leviticus' list of birds Israel must not eat (Leviticus 11:15), and it haunts ruined lands (Isaiah 34:11) and pecks out the eyes of the scornful (Proverbs 30:17). Yet God feeds it. He asks Job, "Who has the raven's meal ready / when its chicks call to God for help" (Job 38:41), and the psalm praises the God who gives "the raven's chicks what they cry out for" (Psalm 147:9). In a famine God tells Elijah, "the ravens have my orders to keep you fed there" (1 Kings 17:4), and they bring him bread and meat morning and evening. Jesus makes the unclean bird an example of trust: "Think about the ravens. They do no sowing and no reaping" (Luke 12:24).
